title: Max Stack
statement:
Build a class `MaxStack`: a stack of integers that can also report and remove its largest value.

- `MaxStack()` starts with an empty stack.
- `push(x)` places `x` on top of the stack.
- `pop()` takes the top value off the stack and returns it.
- `top()` returns the top value and leaves the stack unchanged.
- `peekMax()` returns the largest value currently on the stack and leaves the stack unchanged.
- `popMax()` takes the largest value off the stack and returns it. If that value occurs several times, only the copy nearest the top is removed.

The stack is never empty when `pop`, `top`, `peekMax` or `popMax` is called. Follow-up: make `top` O(1) and every other operation O(log n).
constraints: At most 10^5 calls in total to push, pop, top, peekMax and popMax
The stack holds at least one value whenever pop, top, peekMax or popMax is called
notes:
## Intuition

A plain array handles `push`, `pop` and `top`, but finding and removing the maximum means scanning it: O(n) per call. A max-heap finds the maximum in O(log n) but cannot remove an arbitrary value cheaply. Keep both, sharing one entry object per pushed value, and delete lazily: removing a value from one structure only marks its entry `removed`, and each structure throws marked entries away when they reach its top. Every entry gets an increasing `id`, so among equal values the heap prefers the one pushed last, which is the copy nearest the top of the stack.

## Approach

1. `push(x)` creates `{ value, id, removed }`, appends it to `stack`, and adds it to `heap` with `siftUp`.
2. `topEntry()` pops marked entries off the end of `stack` and returns the live top. `top` reads it; `pop` marks it removed and returns its value.
3. `maxEntry()` removes marked entries from the root of `heap` (move the last element to the root, `siftDown`) and returns the live maximum. `peekMax` reads it; `popMax` marks it removed.
4. `higher(a, b)` orders the heap: larger `value` first, and for equal values the larger `id`.

## Example 1, step by step

- `push(5)`, `push(1)`, `push(5)` create entries with ids 0, 1, 2. The heap root is the 5 with id 2 (same value, newer).
- `top()` returns 5 (id 2). `popMax()` marks id 2 and returns 5; it is still physically in `stack`.
- `top()`: `topEntry` drops the marked id 2 from `stack` and returns 1.
- `peekMax()`: `maxEntry` drops id 2 from the heap root; the new root is the 5 with id 0, so it returns 5.
- `pop()` marks id 1 and returns 1; `top()` drops it and returns 5. Output: `[null, null, null, null, 5, 5, 1, 5, 1, 5]`.

## Complexity

- Time: `push` O(log n); `top` and `pop` amortized O(1); `peekMax` and `popMax` amortized O(log n). Each entry is discarded at most once from each structure.
- Space: O(n) for the entries, including marked ones not yet discarded.

## Pitfalls

- Ties: `popMax` must remove the copy nearest the top, so the heap needs the `id` tie-break; comparing values alone can remove an older copy.
- Mark entries, not values: marking "one 5 is removed" by value breaks when the same number is pushed again later.
- Clean a structure before reading its top; otherwise `top` or `peekMax` can return a value that was already removed through the other structure.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `stack` | entries in push order; the live top is the stack's top |
| `heap` | the same entries as a max-heap by `value`, then `id` |
| `count` | next `id` to hand out |
| `entry` | `{ value, id, removed }` shared by both structures |
| `index`, `parent`, `left`, `right`, `best` | positions inside `heap` while sifting |
